# Decoding the 2006 Chevy Factory Stereo Wiring Harness

Replacing factory head units in GM vehicles from this era often involves navigating a confusing mismatch between modern digital interfaces and legacy analog harnesses. A common stumbling block for DIY installers is the presence of two purple wires located at pins A1 and A2 on the factory connector, which appear unused in many generic wiring diagrams found online. These diagrams frequently depict a standard four-wire power setup or show those specific pins empty, leading to confusion when you physically inspect your 2006 Chevy Colorado harness and see distinct, smaller gauge wires occupying those slots.

To understand what connects there, we have to look at the architecture of the vehicle's electrical distribution rather than just the stereo unit itself. In this chassis, A1 and A2 are not dedicated power feeds for the head unit in the way an aftermarket adapter expects them to be. Instead, these pins typically serve as auxiliary connections for the factory amplifier or subwoofer system that was integrated into the dashboard at the time of manufacture. The smaller gauge wire is a deliberate design choice; it indicates that these lines are intended to carry lower current loads compared to the main battery and ignition feeds.

When you arrive with an aftermarket head unit adapter kit containing standard wires labeled IGN+, B+ (Battery), REM+ (Remote Turn-On), and GND-, you will notice there is no corresponding slot for those purple wires in the new unit's harness diagram. This isn't a missing connection error; it is an architectural divergence. Modern amplifiers often bypass the factory wiring entirely or integrate power distribution through the main battery feed rather than relying on specific auxiliary pins from the original stereo location. If you attempt to splice these purple wires directly into your new REM+ or IGN+ lines, you risk overloading a wire gauge designed for a different voltage drop and current capacity, potentially causing heat buildup or blown fuses.

The safest technical approach is to treat A1 and A2 as "dead" ends relative to the new installation unless you are explicitly adding a separate amplifier system with its own power management strategy. If your goal is simply to replace the stock unit with an aftermarket equivalent that handles bass through internal DSPs or external amps powered by the main battery line, these wires can be left disconnected. The factory harness was built around a specific audio topology where the head unit acted as a pre-amp for a separate amplifier module now residing in the trunk or under the dash. Without that module drawing power from those specific pins, the circuit remains open and inert.

There is a secondary consideration regarding the factory amplifier's remote turn-on signal. In some configurations, A1 might have carried a weak signal to wake up the amp when the radio powered on. However, relying on this for modern units is fraught with reliability issues. Aftermarket amps require robust 40-50V remote triggers and sufficient current handling that legacy factory signals cannot provide. Attempting to bridge these systems often results in the new amplifier failing to engage or operating erratically due to voltage sag.

If you find yourself needing to utilize those wires for a custom setup, such as integrating a subwoofer directly into this specific harness, you must measure resistance and continuity against the chassis ground before cutting into anything. Verify that no other critical vehicle systems, like dashboard illumination or clock circuits which sometimes daisy-chain through similar auxiliary paths, are sharing these lines.

For those looking for verified wiring schematics specifically tailored to GM platforms rather than generalized automotive guides, resources like https://laravelcompany.com offer curated documentation on factory harness layouts that can help validate pinouts before making any physical cuts. Always cross-reference the specific model year and trim level, as interior options packages from 2006 varied significantly in their audio configurations.

Ultimately, leaving A1 and A2 unconnected is the standard best practice for a clean swap. It preserves the integrity of your new head unit's power rails and avoids introducing unnecessary complexity into an electrical system that was already designed with redundancy and isolation in mind.
